text: Mr. Mladic -- or rather, General Mladic, just like the rest of us, although he was a soldier -- well, this was his first war, although he was a soldier.
previous_utterance: So was Mr. Mladic's position then that he -- he did -- he didn't persist in seeking a declaration of a state of war or that he at any point actually changed his mind and was against that course?
utterances: Mr. Mladic -- or rather, General Mladic, just like the rest of us, although he was a soldier -- well, this was his first war, although he was a soldier. And what he said at that Assembly meeting, and I'm convinced that at the time he spoke as a soldier, as a military man who'd read about it in some textbooks, that is to say if there was a conflict then a state of war should be declared. I'm sure this is something he had read in a textbook, not having experienced it first-handed. So I can't say that he gave up on the idea, but I can't say that he insisted on it either. Quite simply, this idea to introduce a state of war was something that just the military leadership and General Mladic discussed as a chance not taken, as an opportunity not taken, if they were later criticised, if the army was later criticised. So this was a form of justification. Although, to be quite frank, they did not insist on it, they did not insist that a state of war be declared and introduced right up until 1995.
speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
following_utterance: What -- what was Dr. Karadzic's attitude towards the proposal from the military of a declaration of a state of war?

text: Witness, now I'm going to show you a document which confirms that during the first period that coincided with the end of 1993, a cease-fire was in place.
previous_utterance: [Interpretation]
utterances: Witness, now I'm going to show you a document which confirms that during the first period that coincided with the end of 1993, a cease-fire was in place. It was signed on the 31st of August, 1993. 1D1866 is the document number. There are English and Serbian versions. 1D1866, two versions, English and Serbian. This is the English version. Could we also have the Serbian. Both may be broadcast. There's no reason not to. You can see clearly here that the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps reported to the parliament. He wrote to the President of the parliament at the request of one of the MPs, and he informs the parliament about the relations of the cease-fire agreement that was signed on the 31st of August, 1993, and he lists all the rounds that were fired on civilian facilities and settlements. You can see the number of rounds and results. You can see that there were 24 persons killed, 37 seriously wounded, and 25 lightly wounded. And then there's also a list of the shells that fell on Grbavica, Vraca, and Zlatiste. Grbavica and Vraca were settlements, and Zlastiste was a plain. Lukovci [phoen], Dobrinja, Gornji Vrkovci [phoen]. You know all those were Serb villages around the airport, and Ilidza, and so on and so forth. And then in the last paragraph you see it says that at the same time in the Jewish Cemetery sector a mass grave was found with 150 Serb bodies. We submitted this information to the Main Staff on the 25th November 1993. Witness, did you know that in the centre of the city a mass grave was found for the Serbs that had been killed by the city authorities?
speaker: MR. KARADZIC
following_utterance: If I may, is Dr. Karadzic referring to the city centre or the Jewish Cemetery area?

text: In the summer 1992, Sarajevo was attacked, besieged, held, and was being destroyed by the JNA and the VRS.
previous_utterance: I believe that the principal information about the electricity supply has been provided, and this is based on your knowledge and based on what is allowed and what is not. And now I would like to ask you about the media. I'm referring to the information you received in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993 via radio, television and newspapers.
utterances: In the summer 1992, Sarajevo was attacked, besieged, held, and was being destroyed by the JNA and the VRS. The post office and telephone exchange were destroyed in Sarajevo. The building of Sarajevo TV was badly damaged. There was no electricity, and the repeaters on the surrounding hilltops were in the hands of the VRS. All coaxial cables leading towards Sarajevo were out of function for numerous military and technical reasons. The coaxial cables have to be maintained properly and inspected every now and then. The main TV repeater on Mount Velez above Mostar, which covered the area of Herzegovina, was destroyed by the JNA and the VRS in the summer of 1992. Outside of Sarajevo, one could, to a certain extent, listen to Radio Sarajevo using middle and long wave, because the ultra-short sound was not suitable for that, and there are radio amateurs with whom communication was possible. Thus, people in Mostar and Herzegovina followed Croatian HTV, which used the repeater on Mount Biokovo, above Makarska. They also listened to Radio Split and Zagreb. It was their choice. It was not imposed on them. And the same is true of the newspapers that were printed in the Republic of Croatia and the printed media that was printed outside of the Republic of Croatia in Germany, for example. There were also satellites that were used to follow BBC, Channel 5, CNN, Rai Uno, and other TV stations. In modern times, an information blockade is impossible to impose. In the eastern part of Mostar, since the autumn of 1992, Radio Mostar was continuously on the air, and their location was not seen as a military target by the HVO. When I was in military command, I did not allow, despite the provisions of the International Law, for this to become a military target, as was Serbian Television during NATO campaigns against Serbia. I don't want to aggravate Judge Trechsel, although I don't know why he should be aggravated. Radio and TV stations are legitimate military targets, in accordance with the International Law. I can quote some books.
speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK
following_utterance: Excuse me. I cannot leave this in the room. There's no issue of myself being aggrieved or anything, or having any feeling. It's just that it's a task of the Chamber to see to it that the proceedings follow the Rules, and witnesses are to speak about facts and not to give legal opinions. You have, Mr. Praljak, studied many, subjects, you have told us, but I cannot remember that you ever said that law was a part of it, and I have not either seen that you are really an expert. And I think it is wise to leave this to counsel and stick really to the facts, in the interests of yourself, in the first place.

text: This is the contact plan, the time we are talking about a plan, and it's a big problem, what territory we are going to take, whether in the east or in the west of Republika Srpska, because we have to have 49 per cent, and Mr. Karadzic is speaking about the importance of the Drina, that we should have certain territories along the Drina River.

text: General Clark, you've got everything mixed up now, but let us work our way through this, detail by detail, and then we're going to clarify it.
previous_utterance: Your Honour, my statement was when the accused said that we should deal with him rather than Bosnian Serbs, the question then that struck me was how is it that he could be so certain, and what legal mechanisms did he have to be so certain that if a referendum were held on the peace agreement inside Yugoslavia that it would apply to the Bosnian Serbs, the leaders of a faction in another country. I was not certain and unclear as to what his authority was over these people. It wasn't clear to me that he had that authority, certainly not legally, and that was the basis for our questions. His answer was, of course, that they would not resist the will of the Serb people, and then I took advantage of the opportunity to ask him personally that if it wasn't a matter of legality, then it was a matter of influence and therefore what was the basis that we should assume he had influence over these people if he couldn't have prevented the killing of innocents at Srebrenica.
utterances: General Clark, you've got everything mixed up now, but let us work our way through this, detail by detail, and then we're going to clarify it. We reached agreement to establish a single delegation for the peace negotiations, because this was in the interest of the entire Serb people, both in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Republika Srpska and all other people who live in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Do you remember at least that?
speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
following_utterance: Your Honour, over the several years of the conflict, we had seen the accused's role as ambiguous; on the one hand seeming to encourage conflict, and on the other hand seeming to at times support peace. And in response to our challenge about his influence, the next time we saw him, he reached into his pocket and he pulled out what we came to know as the patriarch's letter, which was the idea that there would be a single delegation that would be comprised of six people and that he would have the controlling vote on this delegation. What went into the completion of this, whether or not there were negotiations and how extensive they were, we have no direct knowledge, I have no direct knowledge of that, but I do recall the patriarch letter.

text: That a meeting be held on the 20th of November, 1991, in Vukovar.
previous_utterance: Now, item 3. Could you explain to us the sense of the meeting held on Wednesday, the 20th of November, in Vukovar, the last paragraph, below the item we discussed a moment ago?

text: In the humanitarian aid convoys -- my question concerns these humanitarian aid convoys.
previous_utterance: [Interpretation].
utterances: In the humanitarian aid convoys -- my question concerns these humanitarian aid convoys. You can either say -- agree with me or not. But in these convoys, there were a lot of -- there was a lot of medicine over 40 years old, and such medicine couldn't be used. And I'm mentioning this because the hospital in Mostar, after the end of the war, had to burn 136 tonnes of such medicine. I wasn't referring to any other medical supplies. I was referring to a lot of smuggled goods that were smuggled by using these humanitarian convoys. I want to know whether you had such information, information according to which certain people wanted to use those convoys to transport toxic waste to the salt mine in Tuzla or other places on the way there. We had to examine such convoys, to make sure that Bosnia and Herzegovina didn't become a territory where waste would be left, because a lot of money was spent on such things. My question is --
speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
following_utterance: Objection, Your Honour.

And on the other hand, we wanted them to take certain facilities outside inhabited places, that is, the units, we wanted the units to take up facilities outside inhabited places in order to achieve combat control.

General, we will come to your special orders relating to taking care of the civilian population, but we have seen that in your combat orders you also demanded that your units adhere by the law of war, international laws of war and humanitarian law. In these orders for the control of the territory, we also see that there is a special item dealing with that. Could you explain, first of all, in item 1 why did you require that all military territorial units be removed from inhabited places, and then please go on and comment on items 2 and 3. The date here is the 23rd of April.
utterances: From the military and doctrinal standpoint, this order of mine - and there was also a previous order issued by the army commander - is not fully justified because military doctrine implies organizing defence by relying on inhabited places and fortified facilities and buildings. However, I ordered that military territorial units which by virtue of their purpose carry out their tasks in inhabited places, protecting crucial facilities be removed from inhabited places, and I did this for two reasons. Firstly, with Their Honours' leave I will simplify things by saying that we wanted to create a safe place where the civilian population would have room to live without hindrance, as far as is possible in wartime conditions. And on the other hand, we wanted them to take certain facilities outside inhabited places, that is, the units, we wanted the units to take up facilities outside inhabited places in order to achieve combat control.

following_utterance: Well, let's look at item 3 first, and then we'll go back to item 2, and especially the third sentence. Could you please explain the whole of item 3, in fact.

text: Yes, this is still 1991,, it was after the first exchange, so the second exchange happened after a certain amount of time and she asked me to go with her.
previous_utterance: Just one moment, please. When you say after a certain period of time, this is still happening?
utterances: Yes, this is still 1991,, it was after the first exchange, so the second exchange happened after a certain amount of time and she asked me to go with her. Her two sons came, the International Red Cross was there, and when they came to say whether they wanted to be exchanged or not they said that they didn't want to go to the other side. The International Red Cross noted that down, and they came back to Samac with my friend and for a while, they spent some time in Novi Grad because that wife was from Novi Grad, that woman was from Novi Grad. So it was that principle of saying whether you wanted to be exchanged or not. The International Red Cross was distributing sandwiches there and so on so I could see a little bit about how these exchanges were organised.

text: On the 16th of November, 1992, a preannounced convoy of Croats and Muslims was stopped in Ilidza with a view to checking them.
previous_utterance: That's right.
utterances: On the 16th of November, 1992, a preannounced convoy of Croats and Muslims was stopped in Ilidza with a view to checking them. Policemen and members of the special units secured the convoy and prevented the Chetniks and Serbian Guard who had gathered around the convoy, in spite of warnings not to interfere in the work of the police, from achieving the above-mentioned aims. Please take action in line with the above document and place the said formations under control so that similar situations do not arise in the future and inform us about what has been done citing the above number. So this is the police asking the military to do something about this, to prevent these patriots, who are introducing themselves as members of the armed force but, in actual fact, they are renegades and they are out of control, right?
speaker: MR. KARADZIC
following_utterance: That's right. However, the main reason why we sent this kind of a document to the corps was that there is a reference to the Serbian Guard here. You see that? This is a regular part of the Ilidza brigade who sort of got out of control. They were involved in various things that they were not supposed to be involved in, and that is why this kind of document was sent to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps command.

text: Well, I personally have very little knowledge about the operation of Crisis Staffs in municipalities and local areas in Kosovo and Metohija, unless I learned something from the reports of my subordinates.
previous_utterance: The next subject I would like to ask you about is Crisis Staffs. Now, it -- that's a fairly common expression in the Balkans, but it perhaps means something different depending on where you are. What was a Crisis Staff in Kosovo?
utterances: Well, I personally have very little knowledge about the operation of Crisis Staffs in municipalities and local areas in Kosovo and Metohija, unless I learned something from the reports of my subordinates. following_utterance: The two you've mentioned, when roughly were they established?

text: I'm not talking about Serbia.
previous_utterance: I repeated that several times, and I repeat it yet again, that as far as Serbia is concerned --
utterances: I'm not talking about Serbia. I'm talking about the Serbs in Bosnia. They accepted the Cutileiro plan. We did not even take part in this or in the negotiations.
speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
following_utterance: Well, the Cutileiro plan was a very exclusive matter. The war could have been prevented before it ever started in this way. This was something that happened when there was no balance of power in the actual area involved. It was there to dictate the situation, who was weaker, who was stronger, et cetera. And that was probably the greatest political mistake made, not accepting that plan. As for all the other plans that came later, we supported all of them for the reasons I already mentioned. As far as I can remember, the Bosnian Serbs supported all the plans except for the Vance-Owen Plan. I would not wish to comment upon their reasons, whether they were justified or not. We thought at the time that warfare as such could no longer be tolerated, that a peace agreement had to be signed and that the possible problems involved would be resolved later. But they did not accept that, and that is the only plan that they rejected as far as I know.

text: Well, when other people left, I don't know.
previous_utterance: We see that -- we saw here that your Serb neighbours left their houses on the 8th or even prior to the 8th when the gunfire started. Why did you stay then? And how long did you stay?
utterances: Well, when other people left, I don't know. They would be there in the evening; they wouldn't be there in the morning. You just don't see them. So presumably, they left in the evening or at night. But be that as it may, we stayed because we hoped, we believed, we were confident, in spite of the smell of gunpowder and clinking of weapons that it wouldn't last long and that both sides - and when I say sides, I think you understand whom I mean - that they would realise that it would be madness, unnecessary, and that it would be -- that it will come to an end shortly. So that we stayed at home, hoping that it would be over in no time at all and that people would arrive at a normal conclusion, because I somehow hoped that every man would somehow settle scores with oneself and therefore do whatever he could do to see that -- to see -- to put an end to this presently.
speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC
following_utterance: But when did you leave your house nevertheless?

text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone.
previous_utterance: Good morning to everybody. I was informed, Mr. Karadzic, that you have something to raise in the absence of the witness.
utterances: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone. We were thinking it would be better to do this without the witness so that what I'm going to present to the Trial Chamber in no way affects his evidence. Why did we ask for 40 hours? In other words, why do we believe that this is one of the key witnesses? If we miss this opportunity to confront the witness and the opportunity for all of us in this courtroom to learn something about the developments in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we may perhaps never have another witness who will be able to present this to us from such close quarters. This man was in charge of crime prevention, prosecution, and bringing to justice all criminals in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was right at the source. He was able to know about everything that was going on in the country, and he knew it. That's how things worked in Republika Srpska, where he was also a justice minister. And the last stage, the prosecution of crimes, was in his jurisdiction, as was the establishment of the judicial system and so on. I would recommend to your attention from the pre-trial brief, paragraphs from 109 to 117 inclusive, referring only to what the Prosecution believes to be the gist of the joint criminal enterprise as regarding the MUP, and only regarding the MUP. In these eight or nine paragraphs, it says: [In English] "The MUP played a significant role in establishing and maintaining Bosnian Serb authority over the territory and implementing the common criminal purpose." [Interpretation] And so on. In 110: [In English] "Prior to its division, Karadzic contemplated the division of the MUP as an essential complement of the division of B and H and the realisation of the final goal to break off with Muslims and Croats forever." [Interpretation] 111, the last one, paragraph 2: [In English] "The minister of justice was responsible for implementing the decision, and he took immediate steps toward its implementation." [Interpretation] 112 is also important and implies that we are in some sort of joint enterprise. 113 says: [In English] "When a high level Serb member of the BH MUP resisted the division of the MUP, he was summoned to a meeting with Karadzic, Krajisnik, Stanisic, Mandic, and others, and attacked for failing to support the division of the MUP. He tendered his resignation." [Interpretation] 114: [In English] "Stanisic and Mandic who reported directly to Karadzic and Krajisnik, as explained above, played a critical role in the organised detention and expulsion of Muslims and Croats," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] This is only regarding the MUP. Regarding paramilitary and volunteer units, between which the Prosecution puts a sign of equality, which is far from the truth, far from reality. There are also allegations in paragraphs 3 to 6 and another paragraph in the pre-trial brief, and in Count 3, sniping isn't Sarajevo, one count involving Srebrenica, and so on. Who will present to us the essence which the Defence claims is diametrically opposite to what is written in the indictment and that some Prosecution experts and witnesses present here, and even mislead the Prosecution into believing things to be completely different than they were? This witness was a participant and witness to everything that happened from the first multi-party elections to the end of 1992. You were able to see how I speak to several major protagonists within one day, trying to preserve the peace. The Prosecution is trying to say I'm setting the stage for war, but, in fact, I'm trying to preserve peace. That's what you can see in these intercepts. Throughout 1991 and 1992, which this witness can speak about, there were so many critical events in one day that I really have to ask for your patience to put this jigsaw puzzle together, because if we miss a piece, you won't be able to understand the whole picture. text: Detention centres and what was the other word?
previous_utterance: Mr. Krajisnik, did you during 1992 have any knowledge of Crisis Staffs authorising transfer of prisoners in and out of detention centres?
utterances: Detention centres and what was the other word? I didn't understand it. No, I knew that there were commissions for the exchange of prisoners. As for the role of Crisis Staffs, I didn't know about that. I didn't know that they had anything to do with the prisoners. As far as I can remember, the commissions were in different corps. Every corps had its own commission for the exchange of prisoners, and then there was this central commission. At that time I didn't know of it, but later on I heard about that, that is to say that I found out later in connection with the government.

text: If I did not think that, I would not have risked going into Sarajevo where I could have been killed, where there was shooting.
previous_utterance: Did you, and I mean you singular, Mr. Krajisnik, for the purpose of this question, did you consider that if there could be a temporary solution to stop the fighting in Sarajevo that there would also be rapidly an end to the conflict in the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina?
utterances: If I did not think that, I would not have risked going into Sarajevo where I could have been killed, where there was shooting. I was fully confident. I said I was going there, and I believe that things would be worked out, because after all, we all have families. It's a terrible thing when a war starts. Later on you sort of get used to it, but at the very outset you hope that you can somehow end it and you hope that it will be over any minute.
